title: 24 Tips for Leading Better Professional Development
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: After leading more than 100 professional development sessions in 27 states, Dave Stuart Jr. distills what he has learned into a list of 24 loosely ordered tips. He stresses rehearsal, a short and audience-centered introduction, and building credibility, value, belonging and a sense of achievable success in the room. He argues that more minutes do not mean more impact, so workshops should be shortened, new learning front-loaded, and post-lunch sessions made active. The real staying power, in his view, comes from follow-up and a focused, less-but-better slate of topics, ideally delivered in small recurring chunks. He also gives craft advice on slides, humor, citing research as stories, and calls to action that are earned and sparing. He closes by setting the bar at good rather than perfect, since typical PD is weak enough that competence and attentiveness already stand out.
points: Stuart's five key beliefs (credible, valuable, belonging, effort, success) give a facilitator a checklist for the introduction and for the whole session.
He argues that PD length is not impact: shorter days, front-loaded learning and a clear work product beat marathon sessions.
Follow-up and a narrow set of topics matter more than any single event; ideal PD is dripped in about 15 minutes a day for weeks.
Facilitators should name the source of research and tell studies as stories rather than invoking 'the research says'.
Slides are secondary to expertise and rehearsal; keep them visual, don't read them, and aim for good rather than perfect.
quotes: I do this in the car (without slides) and I do this in my hotel room before an event (with slides) — at minimum. This shows me where my thinking is unclear and lets my brain play around with how to organize ideas and lines and so on.

Length of PD is not equal to impact of PD. I always try to let people out early because if I’ve done my job, their brains are tired, and at the end of the day we’ve reached the point of diminishing cognitive returns.

Plus, the impact of a PD is not tied to how many minutes people sit in the room. The impact depends on reflective application throughout and (especially) at the end of the PD, and then follow-up from admin or coaching staff afterwards.

However, at the whole school level there is nothing like developing a system for simple follow-ups on the work, again and again and again, deepening teacher understanding each time. The only way to do this, of course, is to adopt a “less but better” approach to PD.

This is more than a tagline to me. It’s a reminder that virtually every professional development is about achieving more learning in our schools, but such a precious few of them take seriously that teachers are stressed and that every new thing added to a teacher’s list ought to be accompanied by three things the teacher no longer needs to do.

Instead, do your homework and rehearse to the point where you can say where the research comes from. You don’t need to have a bibliography on every screen, but I like to visualize each study that I reference as a story, and sometimes I will tell the actual study design to my audience as if it’s a story.
First of all, professional development in the United States is bad enough that we don’t need to be magnificent or perfect — we just need to be good. Competent. Attentive. Not reading off slides.
